extracted.intended_audience: general readers, academics, comedians, and university communities interested in feminism, controversial humour, and survivor-led performance
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for creating or staging comedy about rape and sexual assault (particularly survivor-performed standup) that aims to challenge rape culture while supporting survivors. Focuses on ethics, craft, audience safety, and political/analytic goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Productive and healing use of jokes about trauma
rubrics_metrics.description: When and how are jokes about difficult or traumatic experiences productive and healing? (quoted question from the page: 'When and how are jokes about difficult or traumatic experiences productive and healing?')
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the humour helps survivors process, enables communication of experience, and contributes to healing rather than retraumatising. The article frames this as a central evaluative question for controversial humour about sexual violence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep theory rooted in real life and real funny jokes
rubrics_metrics.description: Balance academic/theoretical analysis with real-life concerns and comedic effectiveness ('committed to keeping our academic theorizing rooted in real life, real issues, and — of course — real funny jokes').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessors should value both intellectual framing (e.g., feminist analysis, humour theory) and the actual comedic quality; scholarly intent should not replace the need for genuinely funny, grounded performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaningful engagement with privilege, power, and difference
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy can invite meaningful, pleasurable engagements with issues of privilege, power and difference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Material should thoughtfully engage social dynamics (race, gender, sexual difference, etc.) rather than merely exploiting shock; effectiveness includes whether the joke illuminates structural issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Healing power of art and comedy / processing for survivors
rubrics_metrics.description: Making jokes about life — sour parts, sweet parts — can be the best way for some survivors to communicate and process their experience ('RIR&E is about helping survivors process').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the show/function provides therapeutic or processing value to performers and audience survivors, e.g., enabling disclosure, reducing shame, or prompting concrete changes in survivors' lives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid trivialising or endorsing harmful joke genres
rubrics_metrics.description: Reject jokes that trivialize assault (example given: the 'har-har roofies' genre of gags that feminists critique).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Material should not reproduce or celebrate trivialising, celebratory, or permissive depictions of sexual violence; this is an anti-pattern to watch for when judging appropriateness and ethical stance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Performer identity and consent (survivor-led framing)
rubrics_metrics.description: The show featured only survivors and was born of survivors' own choice to talk about their experience (performers are survivors who chose to make it funny).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Priority is given to survivor-led storytelling: performers who are survivors and who consent to using humour about their own experiences. This affects legitimacy and the ethical standing of the material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedic skill and craft
rubrics_metrics.description: RIR&E performers are described as 'skilled standup comics, telling smart-as-sh*t and funny-as-f*ck jokes about their experiences.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effectiveness depends on craft: sharp writing, timing, and performance skill. Strong comedy is necessary for sensitive material to land as intended and to avoid harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience engagement: laughing with vs laughing at
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughing with them at the absurdity of a world that silences survivors and protects perpetrators is described as an act of support and solidarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether audience laughter aligns with solidarity (supporting the performer and message) rather than derision of survivors. The orientation of the audience's response matters ethically and politically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create an atmosphere of solidarity and support
rubrics_metrics.description: The show cultivates an atmosphere of solidarity and support; audiences reported feeling helped and some confided about their own assaults.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess production choices (framing, moderation, workshop elements, community context) for whether they foster safety, allow disclosure, and provide resources or pathways for support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tackling and exposing rape myths
rubrics_metrics.description: The show 'tackles rape myths in hilarious and heartbreaking ways' and exposes how cultural perceptions affect survivors, e.g., jokes that reveal absurdities of rape myths.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether material interrogates and dismantles harmful myths (e.g., 'not raped enough' narratives) rather than reinforcing them; successful work creates new, more accurate narratives about sexual violence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicit content warning / signaling sensitive material
rubrics_metrics.description: The show's title is a blatant sexual assault content warning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use clear warnings or signaling so audiences know what to expect; this is an explicit production choice to help audience preparation and consent to encountering traumatic content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect diversity in grieving and modes of expression
rubrics_metrics.description: Not everyone grieves the same way; some people need to listen, some need silence, others need to laugh.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledge and respect different coping mechanisms; programming and facilitation should not assume a single 'right' response and should provide alternative ways to engage or opt out.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be conscious of external worries and complaints
rubrics_metrics.description: Complaints often come from people worried on survivors' behalf; these worries are rooted in care and compassion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organizers should take such concerns seriously, balancing protection instincts with survivors' agency; anticipate critiques and explain safeguards and rationale for survivor-led comedy.
